content: Newcastle disease is a highly contagious zoonotic disease that affects a wide range of domestic and wild avian species. Its impact is particularly severe in domestic poultry due to their high susceptibility and the potential for devastating effects on the poultry industry during outbreaks. The disease is endemic in many countries. Newcastle disease was first identified in the East Indies in 1926 but was named after Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, where it was rediscovered in 1927. The causative agent of the disease is the Newcastle disease virus (NDV), which is a negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus. Transmission occurs through exposure to fecal matter and other excretions from infected birds, as well as through contact with contaminated feed, water, equipment, and clothing. Humans exposed to infected birds, such as in poultry processing plants, may develop mild conjunctivitis and flu-like symptoms, but the virus does not pose a significant health risk to humans. There has been growing interest in the use of NDV as an anticancer agent due to its ability to selectively kill human tumor cells while exhibiting minimal toxicity to normal cells. The clinical signs of NDV infection vary significantly depending on factors such as the strain of the virus, as well as the health, age, and species of the host. Symptoms may include respiratory signs (such as gasping and coughing), neurological signs (such as depression, loss of appetite, drooping wings, and paralysis), swelling of the eyes and neck, diarrhea, misshapen or thin-shelled eggs, and reduced egg production. NDV strains are classified into three categories based on their virulence: velogenic (highly virulent), mesogenic (intermediate virulence), and lentogenic (non-virulent). Velogenic strains cause severe neurological and respiratory symptoms, spread rapidly, and can result in up to 90% mortality. Mesogenic strains lead to coughing, reduced egg quality and production, and up to 10% mortality. Lentogenic strains produce mild symptoms with negligible mortality. There is no specific treatment for NDV. However, the use of prophylactic vaccines and strict sanitary measures can significantly reduce the likelihood of outbreaks. In 1999, promising results were observed when Newcastle virus was used in cancer patients. The virus, which is naturally attenuated, preferentially targets and replicates in certain types of tumor cells, such as those in the brain and lungs, while sparing normal cells. Researchers tested this novel virotherapy on 14 patients with glioblastoma multiforme and achieved encouraging outcomes for the first time.
